messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Case Vignette: Michael Michael is a nineteen-year-old male who recently experienced a devastating natural disaster. Before the event, he was known for his cheerful and outgoing personality. However, since the traumatic incident, Michael has become distant and withdrawn, struggling to cope with the lasting impact of the disaster. On that fateful day, a powerful tornado swept through his town, destroying homes and businesses in its path. Michael witnessed the complete devastation firsthand as he stood outside his home, watching the wind tear apart familiar structures and seeing people struggle for their lives. The event was seared into his memory with terrifying clarity. Whenever he thinks about that day, he is overwhelmed by the same terror he felt at the time. He can even recall specific smells from that day—the metallic scent of rain and the acrid odor of burning debris—bringing back vivid, distressing images. Since then, Michael has found it increasingly difficult to reconcile his former self with who he feels like now. The person he once was seems unrecognizable; he is no longer the happy young man he used to be. Instead, he often feels a deep sense of despair and a belief that this disaster has permanently changed him for the worse. These negative appraisals have led Michael to adopt several maladaptive strategies in an attempt to cope with his distress. He rehearses conversations before interacting with others, meticulously planning what he will say to avoid any potential embarrassment or stress. In addition, he avoids anything that could be stressful, limiting social interactions and even staying away from places that remind him of the disaster. When thoughts about the event inevitably arise, he tries to suppress them forcefully, but this often leads to a sense of frustration and increased anxiety. The memories of the natural disaster are particularly potent in Michael's daily life. His job as a fast food worker involves frequent customer interactions and dealing with unpredictable situations. The high-pressure environment triggers his maladaptive strategies; he avoids talking to customers unless absolutely necessary and rehearses responses during his breaks, which further isolates him from his coworkers. These avoidance behaviors have led to tangible consequences in Michael’s life. His job performance has suffered because of his heightened stress levels and tendency to avoid any challenging tasks. He has also grown distant from friends who do not understand why he no longer enjoys the same activities as before. The negative appraisals of himself have reinforced these maladaptive strategies, creating a cycle where his fear of further damage leads him to withdraw even more. Michael’s current state is one of profound distress and isolation. What frightens him most is that he feels trapped in this unrecognizable version of himself, with no clear path back to the person he once was. Despite his efforts to suppress thoughts about the disaster, they continue to resurface unexpectedly, heightening his anxiety and confirming his belief that he has permanently changed for the worse. What finally brought Michael to seek help was a growing sense that his current coping strategies were not sustainable and were only making him feel more miserable over time. He is hopeful that with support, he can begin to regain some of the happiness he once knew and find healthier ways to manage his distressing memories and thoughts.
